responsibleOrganization: Comisión Estatal de Servicios Públicos de Ensenada (CESPE)

waterFacilities.locationContext: Ensenada is a coastal city in Baja California that relies heavily on groundwater from the Maneadero and Guadalupe aquifers, supplemented by a seawater desalination plant and imported water.
waterFacilities.systemOverview: The Comisión Estatal de Servicios Públicos de Ensenada (CESPE) operates multiple wastewater treatment plants and a seawater desalination plant. Potable water is supplied via wells, the desalination plant and limited imports.

capacityProfile.description: CESPE operates six wastewater treatment plants treating 22 043 664 m³ of wastewater per year. A seawater desalination plant began operation in 2018 producing 250 L/s (21 600 m³/day) and plans to expand to 500 L/s by 2024.

waterFacilities.operationalDetails: Wastewater plants use biological activated sludge processes; some treat industrial wastewater and require rehabilitation. Treated effluent from El Sauzal, Noreste, El Gallo and El Naranjo is reused for irrigation and aquifer recharge in the Guadalupe Valley. The desalination plant uses reverse osmosis to produce drinking water.
waterFacilities.regulatoryContext: Effluent must comply with NOM‑001‑ECOL‑1996 and permits issued by CONAGUA. The desalination plant must meet NOM‑127 for potable water.
waterFacilities.performanceTrends: Flows vary with tourism and rainfall; some plants operate well below capacity (e.g., Maneadero and Francisco Zarco). Desalination output may increase during drought.

waterQualityIndicators.description: Overall effluent quality meets standards but some plants need rehabilitation to ensure compliance. No specific effluent concentrations are provided.

waterFacilities.energyUsage: Activated sludge processes require aeration; energy use is significant. Desalination is energy‑intensive, consuming electricity for reverse osmosis.
waterFacilities.monitoringMethods: CESPE monitors flow, BOD, TSS and microbial indicators; industrial permits are issued by CONAGUA. Desalination plant monitors salinity, boron and other parameters.
waterFacilities.treatmentTechnologies: Activated sludge, secondary clarifiers, percolation and reuse; desalination uses reverse osmosis and post‑treatment stabilization.
opportunities: Increased reuse of treated wastewater for irrigation and recharge
waterFacilities.dataSources: Ensenada water scarcity analysis and thesis with treatment plant capacities and flows. Lack of publicly available water quality data.

microplastics.locationContext: Ensenada's coastal waters and estuaries may receive microplastics from urban runoff, tourism, fishing and wastewater discharges. The Guadalupe and Maneadero valleys are agricultural areas.
microplastics.systemOverview: No studies have quantified microplastics in Ensenada's drinking water or wastewater effluent. As a coastal city, it is vulnerable to marine debris and microplastic pollution.

concentrationProfile.description: No quantitative data; microplastic concentrations remain unknown. Studies in other Southern California rivers indicate 0.05–16 particles/m³ (Los Angeles River).

microplastics.operationalDetails: Wastewater plants currently do not include microplastic removal technologies. Desalination may remove microplastics through reverse osmosis.
microplastics.regulatoryContext: No Mexican regulations on microplastics; research is emerging. California's policies may influence future regional initiatives.
microplastics.energyUsage: Implementation of microplastic removal would increase energy use; desalination already has high energy demand.
microplastics.monitoringMethods: Standard microplastic sampling (filtration and FTIR) could be used but is not currently practiced.
microplastics.treatmentTechnologies: Advanced tertiary filtration, membrane bioreactors and reverse osmosis could reduce microplastics; coastal clean‑up programs limit plastic waste.
challenges: Marine litter from tourism and fishing
opportunities: Engaging universities and NGOs to study microplastics
Implementing source control and plastic reduction programs
microplastics.dataSources: No Ensenada‑specific data; general reference to Southern California river studies.

waterContamination.locationContext: Groundwater from the Maneadero and Guadalupe aquifers supplies Ensenada; seawater intrusion and agricultural runoff affect quality.
waterContamination.systemOverview: Contaminants include high salinity, nitrates from agriculture, and potential industrial pollutants. Wastewater discharge to the Todos Santos Bay and the Guadalupe Valley influences coastal ecosystems.

contaminantProfile.description: No specific contaminant concentrations published. Agriculture in Maneadero Valley uses treated effluent (~120 L/s) for irrigation of 200 ha. Over‑extraction has led to saline intrusion.

waterContamination.operationalDetails: CESPE blends groundwater with desalinated and imported water to maintain supply. Wastewater plants treat effluent to meet BOD and TSS standards; industrial discharges require permits.
waterContamination.regulatoryContext: NOM‑127 sets drinking water limits; NOM‑001 governs effluent. The city has experienced beach closures due to high bacterial counts linked to wastewater discharges.
waterContamination.performanceTrends: Salinity and nitrate levels fluctuate with rainfall and pumping rates. Beach closures occur periodically after sewer overflows.
waterContamination.waterQualityIndicators: Important parameters include total dissolved solids, chloride, sulfate, nitrate and bacterial indicators. No values reported.
waterContamination.energyUsage: Desalination has high energy consumption; pumping groundwater requires electricity.
waterContamination.monitoringMethods: CESPE monitors drinking water and effluent but results are not publicly detailed. Environmental groups monitor beach water quality.
waterContamination.treatmentTechnologies: Desalination removes salts; planned rehabilitation of wastewater plants will improve effluent quality; recharge of treated effluent helps restore aquifers.
opportunities: Enhancing groundwater recharge with treated effluent
waterContamination.dataSources: Ensenada water scarcity analysis; thesis on industrial wastewater management. Lack of publicly available contaminant data limits assessment.

waterQuality.locationContext: Ensenada's drinking water system combines groundwater from overdrawn aquifers with desalinated seawater and limited imported water.
waterQuality.systemOverview: Water quality varies by source; groundwater is increasingly saline, while desalinated water has low minerals.

qualityProfile.description: No public data for parameters such as pH, TDS, hardness, nitrates or metals. Estimated TDS in groundwater >1 000 mg/L; desalinated water ~200 mg/L.

waterQuality.operationalDetails: Operators blend sources to meet demand and reduce salinity; corrosion control and chlorination maintain distribution safety.
waterQuality.regulatoryContext: Drinking water must comply with NOM‑127; monitoring results are reported to state authorities but not widely shared.
waterQuality.performanceTrends: Salinity and hardness increase during dry seasons; blending ratios change based on aquifer levels and desalination plant output.
waterQuality.waterQualityIndicators: Key indicators likely include high TDS and hardness in groundwater, nitrate from agriculture and residual chlorine. No values published.
waterQuality.energyUsage: Energy use increases with desalination and pumping from deep wells.
waterQuality.monitoringMethods: CESPE monitors pH, TDS, hardness, nitrate and microbial indicators; no microplastic or PFAS monitoring.
waterQuality.treatmentTechnologies: Reverse osmosis desalination; blending; planned upgrades for nutrient removal at wastewater plants.
challenges: Salinity and nitrate pose challenges to drinking water quality
opportunities: Reuse of treated wastewater for recharge
Improved data reporting to guide management
waterQuality.dataSources: Ensenada water scarcity analysis and thesis providing capacity information. No published water quality tables available.
